articles.title: Wu Shicun on why Beijing will not rule out Scarborough Shoal construction
articles.summary:
- Wu Shicun, founding president of China's National Institute for South China Sea Studies, argues that Manila's "assertive transparency" campaign is a deliberate PR strategy: since 2023, the Philippines has intentionally provoked confrontations at Renai Jiao (Second Thomas Shoal) and other features, then disseminated viral videos to frame China as the aggressor, partly to secure Congressional budget and equipment support for its coastguard.

- China has historically concentrated its diplomatic efforts on rule-making frameworks—promoting Code of Conduct (COC) consultations ongoing since 2013 and convening Declaration on the Conduct of Parties (DOC) working group meetings (most recently the 56th session in Vietnam)—rather than engaging in narrative battles.

- Wu acknowledges that China was initially caught off guard by the Philippines' narrative strategy, particularly during the 2023 Second Thomas Shoal stand-off and subsequent intrusions on Sabina Shoal, but says Beijing has since adjusted by proactively clarifying and countering Manila's false narratives.

- As a result, China's overall strategy has undergone a "profound paradigm shift" toward more proactive narrative construction internationally, which Wu frames as a necessary adjustment by a "responsible major power" that must "always tell the truth."

- Wu's title and the interview's framing suggest that Beijing is not ruling out construction at Scarborough Shoal (Huangyan Dao), positioning it as one of several response options against rival claimants' tactics.

articles.title: Zheng Yongnian on Trump, Venezuela and why China doesn’t want ‘a separate kitchen’
articles.summary:
- **Trump's "Donroe Doctrine"**: Political scientist Zheng Yongnian argues Trump is executing a strategic shift from the traditional Monroe Doctrine—focusing on consolidating US influence in the Western Hemisphere while pursuing offshore balancing and strategic contraction from Europe, the Middle East, and East Asia.

- **Domestic-centric "MAGA" strategy**: Unlike previous administrations that discussed strategic retreat (e.g., Obama era), Trump—as a businessman—is seen as capable of follow-through, making the pivot to Latin America and the "backyard" a real possibility rather than mere rhetoric.

- **Venezuela as a catalyst for global restructuring**: Zheng notes the US pivot to Latin America will reshape the regional order and cause disruption, similar to how US withdrawal from established orders in Europe and the Middle East will create local chaos—defining "turbulence" as the trend for coming years.

- **Tripartite partition of world order**: American right-wing think tanks have discussed dividing the world among major powers (the US, Russia, and China). Zheng draws parallels to Putin's long-standing pursuit of the same under different pretexts, with European nations like Poland fearing that a US-Russia compromise over Ukraine would not end Russian ambitions.

- **Rising "regional lords"**: Beyond great power dynamics, middle powers such as Turkey (in Turkic-speaking countries) are also asserting themselves, adding another layer of complexity to the shifting global order.

articles.title: 80 years on from WWII, China’s interests lie in peaceful Asia-Pacific: Rana Mitter
articles.summary:
- Historian Rana Mitter argues WWII's Japanese invasion of China was one of the most important yet underestimated factors in shaping modern China, causing millions of deaths, mass displacement, and the destruction of 1920s–1930s infrastructure.

- The war's devastating economic and social conditions made revolution more likely than reform, enabling the Chinese Communist Party to build strength in the countryside; many socialist-era institutions, such as the work unit system, actually emerged during the wartime period.

- WWII played a key role in China's gradual unification by eliminating rival warlords and bringing nationalist and communist factions together against a common enemy, laying groundwork for the eventual 1949 revolution under Mao Zedong.

- The war also elevated the role of women in Chinese society, with many younger women becoming involved in national defense, health, and nutrition efforts to stabilize families and communities.

- Mitter criticizes Beijing's diplomatic approach, noting China tends to fall back on complaint-driven narratives rather than seizing commemorative opportunities, like the 80th anniversary, to foster substantive people-to-people exchanges with the West.

articles.title: Jeffrey Sachs says US sabre-rattling at China can become self-fulfilling prophecy of war
articles.summary:
• Sachs notes that both the US and China hold economic chokeholds on each other (e.g., rare earths), ensuring neither side can impose its will on the other, so periodic agreements will be reached but frictions will persist, waxing and waning throughout Trump's second term.

• Sachs emphasizes that the US initiated the trade war and must exercise prudence; while some senior US officials are reportedly chastened, Trump's unpredictability and short attention span mean agreements with him are unlikely to hold.

• Sachs advises China not to regard the US or Western Europe as growth markets for exports, predicting the US will restrict Chinese exports regardless; China's export growth should instead focus on Africa, Southeast Asia, South Asia, West Asia, Central Asia, and Latin America.

• Sachs, an economics professor at Columbia University and UN special adviser, acknowledges both sides have strong incentives for cooperation because of mutual gains from trade, and hopes a measure of rationality will prevail despite ongoing tensions.

articles.title: Liu Qian on Chinese innovation, the US rivalry and women holding up half the sky
articles.summary:
• **US-China rivalry extends beyond trade** into technology, ideology, and global collaboration; Liu Qian argues that continued unhealthy competition harms both countries and the global economy.

• **US tariff impact on China is overestimated**: Exports to the US account for only ~2.8% of China's GDP. Even if the entire US export market were wiped out, it would affect only 2-3% of China's economy. Exports overall make up about 19% of GDP, down from a peak of ~36%.

• **China's export portfolio has diversified significantly**: ASEAN is now China's largest export destination (~16% of total exports), surpassing both the US and EU. Exports to Brazil grew 23.3% last year, and exports to Africa rose 25.9% in the first eight months of this year.

• **Exporters have shown resilience**: They have adapted by finding new routes, markets, and products, and exports have generally held steady despite tariff pressures—though longer-term risks remain around unemployment, business confidence, and supply chain adjustments.

articles.title: Fuchsia Dunlop tells how she fell for China’s cuisine and names her perfect dish
articles.summary:
- Fuchsia Dunlop is a British author and chef widely regarded as the Western world's foremost expert on Chinese cuisine, having written seven books on the subject, with a particular focus on Sichuanese food.

- Dunlop first traveled to China in 1994 as a British Council student at Sichuan University and began learning Chinese cooking by studying in local restaurant kitchens and attending the Sichuan Higher Institute of Cuisine, where she later completed a three-month chef's training course alongside 50 Sichuanese students.

- Noting a lack of English-language Sichuan cookbooks, she wrote her first one, published in 2001, filling a significant gap in Western culinary knowledge about the region; Sichuan food has since become widely popular in Britain and beyond.

- She views mooncakes as an important cultural connection to China, particularly when celebrating Mid-Autumn Festival in London, and favours savoury varieties, including Shanghai minced pork mooncakes and Yunnan versions made with ham, sugar, and flaky pastry.

- Dunlop considers Chinese food culture to be vast and endlessly diverse, and she sees writing about it as a compelling way to explore the country and its cultures.

articles.title: South Korea wants free ‘AI for All’. Is society ready?
articles.summary:
- South Korea's President Lee Jae Myung is launching an "AI for All" initiative to provide every citizen free access to AI, integrating it into hospitals, schools, government offices, and daily life, with a 10 trillion won ($7.3 billion) AI budget and an additional 250 billion won allocated through 2027.

- A beta version of free, unlimited-access AI chatbots and agents, developed by consortiums led by SK Telecom, KT, and Kakao using government-lent Nvidia B200 GPUs, is set to launch this month; if successful, it is planned to become a permanent, taxpayer-funded public utility from next year, enabling tasks like booking medical appointments and tax advice via AI.

- The government aims to lower barriers so AI benefits are distributed evenly rather than concentrated among select groups, positioning AI as a public utility akin to infrastructure.

- To manage risks, South Korea relies on its AI Basic Act (effective January), requiring human-in-the-loop oversight, mandatory impact assessments, and synthetic content watermarking, alongside a state-funded AI Safety Institute serving as a technical watchdog and a set of seven "AI Ethics Principles" including accountability, privacy protection, and fairness.

- This aggressive push contrasts sharply with the cautionary stance of leading AI figures such as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton, who have warned of existential risks, while concerns about deepfakes, bias, unemployment, and autonomous weapons continue to grow globally.

articles.title: Hong Kong’s historic vessels sail into the future
articles.summary:
• **Way Foong and Java are rare, historically significant wooden vessels built in Hong Kong in the 1930s** — Way Foong was commissioned by HSBC in 1930 for use as a ferry, tugboat, and pleasure craft, while Java served in the Hong Kong government fleet from 1935, performing duties including VIP transport and anti-piracy patrols.

• **Both vessels were built by the Hong Kong and Whampoa Dock Company**, showcasing the world-class craftsmanship of local shipyards; Java's Burmese-teak construction with deck planks nearly 4.5cm thick earned it a reputation for being "almost unsinkable."

• **The Hong Kong Historic Vessels Foundation (HKHVF), formally founded earlier this year, owns and maintains five historic vessels**, including both Way Foong and Java, with the goal of preserving and promoting Hong Kong's maritime heritage and nurturing future generations of boaters.

• **The organisation's historians have identified nine pre-1950s boats built in Hong Kong**, with some in the HKHVF collection, others privately owned, and one (Mon Lei) whose whereabouts remain unknown; Java was discovered by chance moored in Tai Tam Harbour in the early 2000s, which prompted its purchase and ultimately the foundation's creation.

articles.title: Southeast Asia battles Big Tech to protect children online
articles.summary:
• Indonesia introduced some of Southeast Asia's strictest rules in March 2025, barring under-16s from "high-risk" social media, with Meta, YouTube, and TikTok raising minimum ages to 16 — TikTok alone deactivated 9 million underage accounts by October.

• Enforcement remains challenging: age restrictions rely on platforms' own systems, and many minors still bypass them by lying about their age during registration.

• Indonesia has given tech companies until the end of 2025 to complete self-assessments of their age-verification and child-protection systems, with non-compliance potentially triggering fines of up to 6% of global revenue (roughly US$12 billion for Meta based on 2025 revenue).

• Regional governments beyond Indonesia — including Malaysia, Vietnam, the Philippines, and Singapore — are similarly shifting from urging platforms to act to imposing binding rules on Big Tech regarding child safety online.

• Meta's migration of 22.5 million Indonesian users to restricted "teen accounts" follows a landmark US$18 billion settlement with US states over child harm, but Indonesia's government considers such measures insufficient.

articles.title: Talk is growing of a Tesla-SpaceX merger. Will geopolitics throw a spanner in the works?
articles.summary:
- Tesla's Gigafactory in Shanghai exported over half its production overseas in 2024, setting a record with 7,738 vehicles shipped on a single vessel in July, highlighting the factory's deep integration into Tesla's global supply chain — and its potential vulnerability amid US-China geopolitical tensions.

- Elon Musk faces a balancing act between Tesla's heavy reliance on China for manufacturing and supply chains and SpaceX's role as a core US national security contractor, creating significant regulatory and geopolitical risks in both Washington and Beijing.

- Growing speculation about a potential SpaceX-Texas merger is fueled by deepening technology overlap between the two firms; Tesla supplies solar panels, batteries, and potential Starship components to SpaceX, while SpaceX provides Grok AI and Starlink to Tesla's vehicles and Optimus robot — though Musk has neither confirmed nor denied merger plans.

- Industry observers warn that any merger would intensify geopolitical scrutiny, requiring a complex ring-fenced strategy to satisfy regulators in both the US and China, with an unpredictable geopolitical landscape posing the greatest danger to maintaining this balance.

articles.title: Antwerp: a well-seasoned melting pot of Rubens, diamonds and Belgium’s only Chinatown
articles.summary:
- Antwerp is celebrated for its rich Flemish heritage, notably as the home of Baroque painter Peter Paul Rubens, with masterpieces adorning churches and grand Renaissance architecture reflecting its 16th-century golden age as a global trade capital; the Royal Museum of Fine Arts houses works spanning from Jan van Eyck to René Magritte.

- Beyond its artistic legacy, Antwerp (population 568,000) is a multicultural melting pot shaped by successive waves of immigration: Sephardic Jews expelled from Spain in the late 15th century who established a global diamond trade hub, colonial-era settlers from the Maghreb and Central Africa, post-WWII Chinese immigrants who created Belgium's only official Chinatown, and more recently refugees from Afghanistan, Syria, Iraq, Somalia, and Ukraine.

- The city's late-19th-century Central Station—regularly voted among the world's most beautiful—is located just 40 minutes from Brussels and serves as a gateway to Antwerp's cultural contrasts, with Chinatown's ornamental pagoda gate on one side and the Orthodox Jewish diamond district on the other.

- Within roughly one square mile, about 120 diamond and gold jewelry boutiques operate, sustained by generations of Jewish families; however, some local artisans, such as goldsmith Yosef Degan—who specializes in melting down old gold to create unique designs—describe themselves as among the last authentic craftspeople amid the dense commercial competition.

articles.title: Temu took the world by storm – but has the shopping app lost its thunder?
articles.summary:
- **Temu launched aggressively in the US market**, buying two Super Bowl ad spots in February 2023 at an estimated cost of US$14 million; downloads surged 45% on the day of the campaign, signaling rapid growth.

- **Temu's ultra-low prices relied on two pillars**: leveraging parent company PDD Holdings' deeply mature Chinese supply chain (built through Pinduoduo) and a distribution strategy that allowed the company to avoid hefty import tariffs on goods shipped directly from China to consumers in the US and Europe.

- **China's decades-old manufacturing ecosystem** — characterized by specialized industrial clusters (e.g., electronics in Shenzhen and Dongguan, furniture in Foshan) — gave Temu access to factories and logistics networks producing goods at a scale and cost unmatched globally.

- **Rising global regulation and customs barriers are now eroding Temu's core business model**, making it increasingly difficult and expensive to ship goods directly from Chinese warehouses to Western doorsteps, fundamentally undermining the cost advantage that fueled its growth.

articles.title: Thailand has had enough of foreign tourists behaving badly
articles.summary:
• Tourism accounts for roughly one-fifth of Thailand's economy, yet international visitor numbers remain below their 2019 peak of nearly 40 million — last year saw only 32.9 million arrivals, and the Tourism Authority of Thailand has lowered its 2026 forecast to 30–34 million due to geopolitical conflicts driving up oil prices and airfares.

• The post-Covid tourism landscape has shifted structurally: large Chinese tour groups have largely disappeared, replaced by smaller "free, independent travellers" (FITs), leaving many traditional tourist-dependent businesses — like a 90-year-old crocodile farm near Bangkok — struggling to adapt.

• A strong Thai baht has pushed budget-conscious travellers toward cheaper alternatives in Vietnam and Malaysia, further compounding Thailand's visitor shortfall despite a 60-day visa-free scheme introduced in 2024 to attract tourists back.

• The article's title suggests that growing frustration over misbehaving foreign tourists is also eroding Thailand's welcoming posture, though the specific details on this point are cut off from the provided text.

articles.title: Going ‘car-lite’: why more Singaporeans are quitting driving
articles.summary:
- **Surging costs are driving Singaporeans to abandon car ownership**: Certificate of Entitlement (COE) renewal costs have skyrocketed from S$10,000 in 2006 to over S$112,000 by 2024, compounded by rising road tax, fuel, maintenance, insurance, and electronic road pricing (ERP) charges.

- **Privately owned car numbers have hit a multi-year low**: Government figures from July 2024 show 516,237 privately owned cars — the lowest since 2019 — though they still make up 79% of all vehicles on the road; rental and ride-hailing car numbers have risen in the interim.

- **Singapore is pursuing a "car-lite" policy through infrastructure investment and demand management**: The Land Transport Authority's "Move Lite" campaign (launched 2022) promotes walking, cycling, and public transport, shifting messaging from highlighting alternatives to spotlighting driving's downsides such as congestion and parking hassles.

- **Congestion pricing is being expanded**: ERP charges returned to the Orchard Road district in August 2024 for the first time since the pandemic began, as part of broader efforts to manage road usage in the land-scarce city-state.

articles.title: Chinese brokers work to crack the final code: win clients on global stage
articles.summary:
- **China's financial ambitions have evolved beyond emulating Wall Street**: President Xi Jinping called in 2023 for cultivating first-class investment institutions with "distinct Chinese characteristics," signaling a shift from copying Western models to building an independent financial superpower.

- **Strong domestic foundation established**: China now has the world's second-largest capital market after the US, and direct financing through stocks and bonds surpassed bank lending for the first time in 2025, creating favorable conditions for domestic securities firms.

- **Overseas expansion is the next frontier**: With Hong Kong's growing role and mainland companies investing more aggressively abroad, Chinese brokerages are increasingly pushing into international markets as a key growth driver, per Fitch Ratings.

- **Decades-long journey from apprentice to contender**: Since CICC's founding in 1995 as China's first Sino-foreign JV investment bank, Chinese firms have progressed from learning basic mechanics from Western banks (e.g., Goldman Sachs mentoring CICC ahead of China Mobile's US$4.2 billion Hong Kong/NY listing in 1997) to acquiring the networks and capabilities needed to compete globally.

commentary:
# 泰国旅游业的困境：全球资本主义体系中的"微笑经济"之殇

**一、现象描述**

泰国旅游业遭遇游客人数下滑与外国游客失当行为双重冲击，疫后复苏乏力，经济支柱面临结构性危机。

**二、政治经济学定位**

泰国旅游业约占国民经济的五分之一，这一惊人比例绝非偶然。它深刻揭示了一个后发资本主义国家在全球资本积累体系中的依附性位置。旅游业本质上是一种商品化了的服务出口：泰国将本国劳动力、自然资源与空间景观打包为可供国际资本流通消费的"旅游商品"。正如马克思所言，**"资本主义生产不仅是商品的生产，它实质上是剩余价值的生产"**（《资本论》第一卷·第五章）。泰国旅游业的运作逻辑正是如此——它将服务业劳动的价值增殖过程高度依赖于外部需求，其"价值形成过程"必须通过外国游客的消费才能转化为"价值增殖过程"。当中国、俄罗斯等国的"大规模大众旅游"退潮，当泰铢走强、航空燃油价格上涨挤压国际资本流向东南亚的意愿时，这条依附性价值链便迅速暴露其脆弱本质。

**三、深层结构分析**

从生产组织形式看，泰国旅游业呈现出马克思所描述的资本主义劳动协作的典型特征。**"较多的工人在同一时间、同一空间，为了生产同种商品，在同一资本家的指挥下工作，这在历史上和逻辑上都是资本主义生产的起点"**（《资本论》第一卷·第十一至十三章）。从普吉岛的五星级度假村到芭提雅的水上摩托经营者，从曼谷的按摩店到鳄鱼养殖场，数以万计的泰国劳动者被组织在"旅游资本"的统一指挥之下，以协作劳动的形式生产着可供国际消费的服务商品。然而，这种协作的新型生产力——"集体力"——的创造者恰恰是劳动者自身，而其成果却被旅游资本家和跨国旅游中介所占有。疫情后，游客从大型旅行团（大巴士旅游模式）转向独立自由行（FIT模式），这一消费方式的转变实际上重构了旅游资本的剥削形态：从对集体劳动的集中剥削转向对分散化、碎片化服务劳动的更加隐性的榨取。而正如马克思所深刻指出的，**"工场手工业同时也损害了工人的整个劳动能力，使工人畸形发展"**——泰国旅游经济的长期畸形发展，正使整个国民经济结构丧失了多元化生产能力，沦为国际消费市场波动的附庸。**"机器大工业使工人从机器的附属物变成了机器体系的附属物"**，泰国的旅游从业者又何尝不是全球旅游资本机器体系中的附属物？

**四、阶级与利益分析**

在此结构中，受益者是掌握旅游资本的泰国本土资产阶级、跨国旅游集团与航空业寡头；直接受损者则是从事低薪、不稳定服务劳动的广大泰国底层劳动者——导游、按摩师、水上运动经营者、小商贩等，他们承受着劳动的高风险与收入的高度不确定性。与此同时，泰国社会整体作为"国家"单位承受着主权被经济结构绑架的代价：政策制定被旅游资本的利益所左右，自然资源和公共空间被让渡给外国消费资本的逻辑。权力在这一过程中从泰国国家向国际资本流动——游客的不当行为实质上是全球不平等交换关系的微观投射。

**五、主流叙事批判**

泰国官方与主流媒体的叙事框架将问题定性为"游客行为失当"和"国家形象管理"，泰国旅游局则通过签证优惠等技术手段试图"修复"游客数量。这种叙事巧妙地遮蔽了矛盾的实质：它将结构性的不平等交换关系——即后发国家以廉价劳动力和自然资源向国际消费市场出口服务商品的依附性地位——转化为道德层面的"文明教养"问题。"微笑之国"的国族话语将剥削性的劳动关系美化为文化特质，仿佛泰国服务业劳动者低薪高强度的"微笑服务"是一种天然的文化禀赋而非资本积累的强制结果。游客的不当行为固然需要约束，但将其作为危机的核心叙事，无异于以现象掩盖本质。

**六、解放前景**

泰国旅游业危机的出路，不在于更多签证优惠或更严厉的执法，而在于从根本上改变旅游经济的生产关系：推动旅游业生产资料的社会化——将关键旅游资源纳入民主管理的合作社体系；发展多元化的民族经济以降低对单一依附性出口部门的依赖；保障旅游服务业劳动者的组织权和集体谈判权，使其不再沦为国际消费资本机器体系的附属物。唯有如此，泰国劳动者才能从被"旅游资本"所消费的劳动力商品，回归为经济生活的主体。
